rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Equilibrium is chemistry's steady state: opposing processes running **at equal rates** so that nothing observable changes while everything molecular continues. A **reversible reaction** in a closed vessel marches toward that tie automatically — forward rate falling, reverse rate climbing, crossing at equilibrium.…

rows.text: ***The sealed soda bottle*** — CO₂ dissolves and escapes at equal rates; open the cap, the dissolved gas rushes out because the equilibrium that held it is destroyed.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Rates equal, concentrations constant, not equal". Catalyst = faster arrival, same destination. Tracer test = dynamism proof. Physical = phase; chemical = new substances.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Distinguish physical and chemical equilibrium with one example each, and explain why chemical equilibrium is called dynamic.** — **Physical equilibrium** is established between two states of the same substance, with no new substances formed: in a closed flask at constant temperature, water evaporates at the same rate as…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): State four characteristics of chemical equilibrium.** — **(1) Constancy of composition:** the concentrations of all reactants and products become and remain constant (though not necessarily equal to each other). **(2) Dynamic activity:** the forward and reverse reactions continue indefinitely at equal rates.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: For "dynamic nature" answers, always include the tracer evidence — it converts a assertion into a proof and examiners reserve a mark for it.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Equal rates, not equal amounts — the whole quantitative story of topics 53–55 flows from this one sentence: Kc measures the constant ratio the tied rates produce.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Reversible reaction: both directions at once (⇌); closed system required. Physical equilibrium: phase change, no new substances (H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂O(g)); chemical: recomposition (CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂). Dynamic: equal opposing rates, constant composition, tracer-proven.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Haemoglobin + O₂ ⇌ oxyhaemoglobin in blood is a physiological equilibrium — altitude shifts it, which is why climbers pant and why oxygen masks exist.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Why can a reversible reaction never go to completion in a closed vessel?** — In a closed vessel the products cannot escape, so as the forward reaction runs, products accumulate and begin to react backwards.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Reactions That Refuse to Finish Most reactions in a closed flask never "complete": forward and reverse processes run side by side until their rates tie. That tie is **equilibrium** — dynamic, not dead.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Reversible reactions and the approach to equilibrium - A **reversible reaction** proceeds in both directions simultaneously, written with the double arrow ⇌: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. - Starting from reactants only, the forward rate is initially maximal and falls as reactants deplete; the reverse rate starts at zero and climbs as products accumulate.…  ·  ## 3. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).  ·  ❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.  ·  ❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.  ·  ❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).  ·  ❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...  ·  ❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.  ·  ❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.  ·  ❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.  ·  ❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.  ·  ❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).  ·  ❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
